analysis.one_liner: Adds outpatient prescription drug coverage to Medicare, delivered through competitively bid private contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee for 20 months and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1999 Medicare paid for hospital and doctor care but not the prescription drugs seniors fill at the pharmacy. This bill would have added outpatient drug coverage to Medicare Part B: beneficiaries would pay a $200 yearly deductible and 20% coinsurance, with coverage fully kicking in once their own out-of-pocket spending hit $3,000 a year. Instead of the government running the benefit directly, private companies (including pharmacy benefit managers, pharmacy delivery systems, and insurers) would compete for regional contracts, and their prices would have to match what large private employers pay. It also expanded help for low-income seniors through Medicaid, let retirees keep equivalent employer drug coverage, and removed the time limit on Medicare coverage of anti-rejection drugs for transplant patients.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who today pay cash at the pharmacy, especially the roughly one in three seniors who lacked any drug coverage in 1999; low-income seniors who would gain Medicaid help with premiums and a full wrap-around drug benefit; transplant recipients who would no longer lose anti-rejection drug coverage after a time limit; and retirees whose employer plans would get federal payments for keeping them covered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors paying full price for prescriptions

how_it_helps.text: Adds coverage of outpatient prescription drugs, biologics, and insulin to Medicare Part B, which previously paid for drugs only in limited settings like hospitals [S2][S3].
Caps what a beneficiary can be forced to pay out of pocket: after reaching $3,000 in yearly cost-sharing, the copayment drops to zero [S3].
Uses competitive bidding with a benchmark requiring that average drug costs match what large private-sector purchasers pay, an attempt to capture private-sector-negotiated prices for Medicare [S3].
Raises Medicaid income eligibility for Medicare cost-sharing help from 120% to 135% of poverty and adds a prescription drug wrap-around benefit for low-income Medicare beneficiaries [S2][S3].
Eliminates the time limit on Medicare coverage of immunosuppressive drugs, so transplant patients would not lose anti-rejection drug coverage [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The financing comes through the Medicare Part B system: enrollees' monthly premiums would rise to cover the drug benefit (with waivers for people who already had equivalent coverage), beneficiaries pay the new deductible and coinsurance, and general revenue picks up its usual share of Part B costs. Drug makers would bear lower negotiated prices through formularies, generic substitution, and competitive bidding.

drawbacks.text: The cost-sharing design is steep: a $200 deductible applies before any coverage begins, the beneficiary pays 20% of drug costs up to $1,700 in total yearly drug spending, and coverage is complete only after $3,000 out of pocket — meaning seniors with moderate drug needs pay a large share themselves [S3].

Contractors may use formularies and charge higher cost-sharing for non-formulary drugs, and the bill leaves the financing implicit in higher Part B premiums rather than creating a dedicated funding source [S3].

Requiring beneficiaries to enroll with a private contractor, with automatic assignment if they fail to choose, creates the potential for plan churn, limited pharmacy networks, and access gaps in areas where few entities bid [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors with no drug coverage, the bill offered something Medicare did not provide at all in 1999, with a hard out-of-pocket cap for the sickest patients — a large gain against real but manageable costs. Its weak points were the heavy cost-sharing in the middle range and its reliance on premium increases and private contractors rather than direct public administration. On balance the benefits to uninsured seniors clearly outweighed the design flaws, though a more generous or more simply structured benefit would have served them better.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 1999 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on April 20, 1999, joined by Sens. Rockefeller and Wellstone [S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action of any kind followed — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — beyond two rounds of introductory remarks by the sponsor, the last in September 2000 [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, seniors continued to pay cash retail prices for prescriptions, and drug makers avoided the competitive bidding, formulary, and generic-substitution pressures the bill would have imposed. Pharmacy benefit managers and insurers avoided a government-run bidding system that could have constrained how the future drug benefit business was structured.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the floor in April 1999 and again in September 2000

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. William Roth (R-DE)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving the bill to die when the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed government-administered Medicare drug benefit proposals of this era, favoring coverage added through private insurers instead.

sides.party_line_note: All five Senate supporters — the sponsor and four cosponsors — were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors; no roll-call votes were ever taken.

industries.note: Competitive bidding benchmarked to large private purchasers, formularies, and mandatory generic substitution would have pushed down the prices Medicare paid for drugs. Beneficiaries' gain from affordable drugs comes directly out of manufacturers' pricing power.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: The bill makes private companies — PBMs are named first among eligible entities — the permanent delivery channel for a new public drug benefit, winning multi-year regional contracts paid by Medicare. Public money flows through them even as they are regulated.

Contractors must offer services through a sufficient network of retail pharmacies and must compensate pharmacists for patient counseling, creating new demand, but network contracting would also give contractors leverage over reimbursement.

Medigap policies would have to offer drug coverage that complements rather than duplicates the new Medicare benefit, reshaping a product line that had often included (or charged heavily for) drug coverage.
